questions.question: Which statement best captures bilinearity of a pairing e : G1 × G2 → GT?
options: e(a·P, b·Q) = e(P, Q)^(a·b) for scalars a, b
e(P, Q) = e(Q, P) for all inputs
e(P + Q, R) = e(P, R) + e(Q, R) as integers
e(P, Q) outputs a point in G1
questions.explanation: Bilinearity means the pairing is linear in each input, letting scalars move into the exponent in GT.

questions.question: In the core BLS scheme, what is the signature on a message m under secret key sk?
options: sig = sk·H(m), a group element (point) in the signing group
sig = H(sk || m), a 32-byte hash
sig = H(m)^(-sk), an inverse in GT
sig = (r, s) like ECDSA
questions.explanation: BLS signs by multiplying the hash-to-curve point by the secret scalar, producing a single group element signature.

questions.question: Why does BLS verification check e(sig, G2) == e(H(m), pk)?
options: Because bilinearity implies e(sk·H(m), G2) = e(H(m), sk·G2)
Because hash functions are collision resistant
Because pk is a hash of sig
Because e is symmetric so inputs can be swapped freely
questions.explanation: The check is exactly the bilinear identity with pk = sk·G2 and sig = sk·H(m).

questions.question: In the basic BLS aggregate signature scheme, what rule is required to prevent rogue-key issues?
options: All messages in the aggregate must be distinct
All public keys must be identical
All signatures must include a random nonce
All messages must be empty strings
questions.explanation: The basic scheme defends against rogue-key attacks by enforcing message distinctness in AggregateVerify.

questions.question: Attack concept: what is a 'rogue-key attack' in same-message BLS multi-signatures?
options: An attacker crafts a public key dependent on others so a forged aggregate verifies without all signers participating
An attacker recovers sk from pk by solving a hash preimage
An attacker flips a bit in a signature and it still verifies
An attacker forces the pairing output to be 1 for all inputs
questions.explanation: If you allow fast same-message aggregation without defenses, a maliciously chosen public key can make a forged aggregate signature verify.

questions.question: Which mechanism is commonly used to enable fast same-message aggregation safely?
options: Require a proof of possession (PoP) for each public key
Switch from SHA-256 to MD5
Encode points in base58 instead of bytes
Disable hashing-to-curve and sign raw messages
questions.explanation: PoP ties each registered public key to a signer who knows the corresponding secret key, blocking rogue-key constructions.

questions.question: Why must BLS implementations specify a concrete hash-to-curve ciphersuite / domain separation tag?
options: So different protocols can't accidentally interpret the same bytes as the same group element
So signatures become randomized instead of deterministic
So aggregation becomes impossible
So subgroup checks are no longer needed
questions.explanation: Domain separation makes the hash-to-curve mapping protocol-specific, preventing cross-protocol reuse and mismatched hashing.

questions.question: What is the most important validation step when deserializing BLS public keys or signatures in real libraries?
options: Ensure the point is in the correct prime-order subgroup (including cofactor/subgroup checks)
Ensure the bytes are ASCII
Ensure the point has an x-coordinate less than y
Ensure the signature is probabilistic
questions.explanation: Pairing curves have cofactors and multiple subgroups; accepting points outside the intended subgroup can break security or consensus.
